claim: The death of a romantic partner is cited as one of the most traumatic experiences in a person's life and results in grief and corresponding indicators of mental and physiological distress.
source: The death of a romantic partner is cited as one of the most traumatic experiences in a person's life and results in grief and corresponding indicators of mental and physiological distress (Keyes et al., 2014; Holmes and Rahe, 1967).
evidence: Supported by citations to Keyes et al., 2014 and Holmes and Rahe, 1967

claim: For the majority of people acute grief subsides within approximately six months as the bereaved integrates and adapts to the loss.
source: However, for the majority of people acute grief subsides within approximately six months as the bereaved integrates and adapts to the loss (Shear et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shear et al., 2011

claim: Most people will eventually form a new pair bond, which provides a behavioral indicator of loss adaptation.
source: Most people will also eventually form a new pair bond, which provides a behavioral indicator of loss adaptation (Shear and Shair, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shear and Shair, 2005

claim: The processes that enable loss adaptation remain poorly understood but likely occur via the same neural systems that are uniquely engaged by pair bonding.
source: The processes that enable such adaptation remain poorly understood but likely occur via the same neural systems that are uniquely engaged by pair bonding (Blocker and Ophir, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blocker and Ophir, 2016

claim: Socially monogamous prairie voles recapitulate many aspects of human social bonds, making them ideal for interrogating the neurobiology of bonding and loss.
source: Socially monogamous prairie voles are a laboratory-amenable species that recapitulates many aspects of human social bonds, making them ideal for interrogating the neurobiology of bonding and loss.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about prairie voles as a model organism

claim: Pair bonded voles will prefer to affiliate with their partner, display selective aggression towards non-partner individuals, and exhibit robust and organized biparental care.
source: Pair bonded voles will prefer to affiliate with their partner, display selective aggression towards non-partner individuals, and exhibit robust and organized biparental care (Williams, 1992; Getz et al., 1981; Williams et al., 1992; Insel and Young, 2001; Carter et al., 1995; Winslow et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Williams, 1992; Getz et al., 1981; Williams et al., 1992; Insel and Young, 2001; Carter et al., 1995; Winslow et al., 1993

claim: The nucleus accumbens is a critical hub that is engaged when forming a bond and is implicated in loss processing.
source: While an extended network of brain regions mediates social processing and decision making, the nucleus accumbens (NAc)—a region important for reward, motivation, and action selection—is a critical hub that is engaged when forming a bond and is implicated in loss processing (Aragona and Wang, 2004; Lim and Young, 2004; Walum and Young, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aragona and Wang, 2004; Lim and Young, 2004; Walum and Young, 2018

claim: In humans, holding hands with a romantic partner enhanced blood oxygenation levels (BOLD) in the NAc.
source: In humans, holding hands with a romantic partner enhanced blood oxygenation levels (BOLD) in the NAc and successful adaptation to spousal loss is associated with a reduced partner-associated BOLD signal in this region (O'Connor et al., 2008; Kreuder et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Connor et al., 2008; Kreuder et al., 2017

claim: Successful adaptation to spousal loss is associated with a reduced partner-associated BOLD signal in the nucleus accumbens.
source: In humans, holding hands with a romantic partner enhanced blood oxygenation levels (BOLD) in the NAc and successful adaptation to spousal loss is associated with a reduced partner-associated BOLD signal in this region (O'Connor et al., 2008; Kreuder et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Connor et al., 2008; Kreuder et al., 2017

claim: When separated from their partner, prairie voles exhibit behavioral and physiological distress that mirrors what is seen upon bond disruption in humans and other species.
source: Further, when separated from their partner, prairie voles exhibit behavioral and physiological distress that mirrors what is seen upon bond disruption in humans and other species, such as titi monkeys (Carter et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carter et al., 1995

claim: Partner separation in prairie voles results in increased circulating glucocorticoid levels, activation of the HPA axis, increased anxiety, decreased pain thresholds, and autonomic dysfunction.
source: These include increased circulating glucocortioids levels, activation of the HPA axis, increased anxiety, decreased pain thresholds, and autonomic dysfunction (McNeal et al., 2014; Grippo et al., 2007; Bosch et al., 2016; Pohl et al., 2019; Osako et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to McNeal et al., 2014; Grippo et al., 2007; Bosch et al., 2016; Pohl et al., 2019; Osako et al., 2018

claim: If a pair bonded prairie vole loses their partner, given enough time, they will form a new bond that supersedes the original bond.
source: However, we have previously shown that if a pair bonded prairie vole loses their partner, given enough time, they will form a new bond that supersedes the original bond (Harbert et al., 2020; Tamarin et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harbert et al., 2020; Tamarin et al., 1990

claim: Male voles are able to form a new pair bond 4 weeks post-separation, but not 2 weeks or earlier.
source: Prior work has shown that male voles are able to form a new pair bond 4 weeks post-separation, but not 2 weeks or earlier (Harbert et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harbert et al., 2020

claim: Opposite-sex and same-sex paired males demonstrated a partner preference even after extended separation.
source: In contrast to our initial hypothesis, we found that opposite-sex and same-sex paired males demonstrated a partner preference even after extended separation (Figure 1B; Lee et al., 2019; Goodwin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and citations to Lee et al., 2019; Goodwin et al., 2019

claim: Both opposite-sex and same-sex pairs form a selective preference for their partner after 2 weeks of pairing.
source: In pairs that remained with their partners throughout the 6-week timeline, both opposite-sex and same-sex pairs form a selective preference for their partner after 2 weeks of pairing (Figure 1B, one sample t-test relative to 50%: opposite-sex p=0.00564, same–sex p=0.00922).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The baseline partner preference for both opposite- and same-sex pairs is retained and even moderately strengthened after 4 additional weeks of cohabitation.
source: The baseline partner preference for both opposite- and same-sex pairs is retained—and even moderately strengthened—after 4 additional weeks of cohabitation (one sample t-test relative to 50% for 48 hr PPT: opposite-sex p=0.0107, same-sex p=0.01478; for 4 weeks PPT: opposite-sex p=5.19 × 10-7, same-sex p=6.49 × 10–7, two-way RM-ANOVA in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis including t-tests and ANOVA

claim: Both opposite-sex and same-sex pairs retain their partner preference after short-term and long-term separation.
source: In separated animals, both opposite-sex and same-sex pairs form a selective preference for their partner after 2 weeks of cohabitation (one sample t-test relative to 50% short-term separated animals: opposite-sex p=3.30 × 10–12, same-sex p=7.72 × 10–5; long-term separated animals: opposite-sex p=1.50 × 10–3, same-sex p=3.04 × 10–5) and retain their partner preference after short-term and long-term separation (one sample t-test relative to 50%: short-term separated animals: opposite-sex p=4.10 × 10–7, same-sex p=3.66 × 10–8; long-term separated animals: opposite-sex p=0.001846, same-sex p=3.14 × 10–8).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis including t-tests

claim: There was no significant difference in partner preference score due to either separation duration or partner type.
source: Additionally, there was no significant difference in partner preference score due to either separation duration or partner type (Figure 1B; two-way RM-ANOVA with repeated measures for timepoint: short-term separation: Main effect of partner (opposite- vs same-sex): F(1,28) = 0.38, p=0.54; Main effect of time: F(1,28) = 0.22, p=0.64; Partner X time: F(1, 28)=1.87, p=0.18; long-term separation: Main effect of partner (opposite- vs same-sex): F(1,26) = 1.70, p=0.20; Main effect of time: F(1,26) = 0.16, p=0.70; Partner X time: F(1, 26)=0.057, p=0.81).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (two-way RM-ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Partner huddle increases with extended co-housing in both opposite-sex and same-sex pairing types, indicating a strengthening of partner-directed affiliation.
source: Of note, partner huddle increases with extended co-housing in both pairing types indicting a strengthening of partner-directed affiliation (2-way RM-ANOVA: main effect of timepoint (4 wks:base): F(2, 42)=4.92, p=0.012, η=0.170) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (2-way RM-ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The increase in partner huddle over time was not observed in opposite-sex or same-sex paired males that had been separated from their partner.
source: This increase was not observed in opposite-sex or same-sex paired males that had been separated from their partner (Figure 1D and E; two-way RM-ANOVA in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (two-way RM-ANOVA) and data shown in Figures 1D and E

claim: Long-term separation effectively impedes the maturation and strengthening of the pair bond without necessarily dissolving the baseline preference.
source: This suggests that long-term separation effectively impedes the maturation and strengthening of the pair bond without necessarily dissolving the baseline preference.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing maintained preference but lack of strengthening after separation

claim: Opposite-sex males that remain paired exhibited increased partner huddle duration at 4 weeks relative to baseline, which was not observed in opposite-sex separated males.
source: However, at the long-term timepoint, we observed another indicator that separation impedes ongoing pair bond strengthening: opposite-sex males that remain paired exhibited increased partner huddle duration at 4 weeks relative to baseline, which was not observed in opposite-sex separated males (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: In same sex paired males, ongoing pairing was not required for increased partner huddle at the long-term timepoint.
source: In contrast, in same sex paired males, ongoing pairing was not required for increased partner huddle at the long-term timepoint (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: The transcriptional differences for opposite- versus same-sex pairs were strikingly similar following either 2 or 6 weeks of pairing.
source: When ordering transcripts based on their log2FoldChange at the short-term timepoint, the global transcriptional differences for opposite- versus same-sex pairs were strikingly similar following either 2 or 6 weeks of pairing, suggesting stable pair bond associated transcription across these timepoints (Figure 2D; Spearman's Rho = 0.38, p=2.2 × 10–16).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Spearman's correlation) and data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The observed correlation in gene expression across short and long-term pairing timepoints is greater than would be expected by chance.
source: We further determined that the observed correlation across timepoints is stronger than what would be expected by chance. We shuffled each animal's cohort identity at the long-term timepoint and calculated Rho values of the log2FoldChange of differential gene expression between the observed short-term pair bond and the shuffled long-term pair bond over 1000 iterations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by permutation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D

claim: The observed Rho value was greater than 100% of iterations, indicating that the similarity in gene expression across short and long-term pairing timepoints is greater than would be expected by chance.
source: Our observed Rho value was greater than 100% of iterations, indicating that the similarity in gene expression across short and long-term pairing timepoints is greater than would be expected by chance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by permutation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: There was significant overlap in the upregulated and downregulated transcripts across short-term and long-term pairing timepoints.
source: There was significant overlap in the upregulated (104 shared, Fisher's Exact Test: χ2=30.24, p=5.36 X 10–31) and downregulated (46 shared, Fisher's Exact Test: χ2=13.32, p=7.05 X 10–14) transcripts across timepoints (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Fisher's Exact Test) and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E

claim: RRHO analyses demonstrated extensive concordance of transcriptional patterns between 2- and 6-week paired voles.
source: We observed extensive concordance of transcriptional patterns between 2- and 6-week paired voles, further supporting that the transcriptional profile of pair bonds is stable (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by RRHO analysis shown in Figure 2F

claim: Upregulated transcripts in pair bonded males are associated with glia and extracellular matrix organization.
source: Combined pair bond GO terms associated with the upregulated DEGs and the quadrant UU genes strongly implicate changes in glial cells and extracellular matrix organization (Figure 2H), which is mirrored by activation of glioblastoma signaling via IPA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by GO and IPA analysis shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: Downregulated transcripts in pair bonded males are associated with nucleoside synthesis and synaptic plasticity.
source: Combined pair bond GO terms associated with the downregulated DEGs and the quadrant DD genes are implicated in nucleoside synthesis and synaptic plasticity (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2H

claim: IPA indicates a suppression of corticotropin releasing hormone signaling in pair bonded voles.
source: IPA indicates a suppression of corticotropin releasing hormone signaling, potentially reflecting the strong social buffering of stressors that occurs in pair bonded voles specifically (Bosch et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2013; Bosch et al., 2009; Smith and Wang, 2014; Burkett et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and citations to Bosch et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2013; Bosch et al., 2009; Smith and Wang, 2014; Burkett et al., 2016

claim: The pair bond signature remains largely concordant after short-term separation.
source: We found that the pair bond signature remains largely concordant after short-term separation as indicated by significant signal among upregulated genes (quadrant UU), and to a lesser extent, downregulated genes (quadrant DD; Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by RRHO analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: Following long-term separation, the pair bond gene signature is largely undetectable.
source: However, following long-term separation, the pair bond gene signature is largely undetectable as indicated by a lack of significant signal throughout the RRHO plot.
evidence: Inferred from RRHO analysis results

claim: There were significantly more shared DEGs between the combined pair bond group and short-term separation group than would be expected by chance.
source: There were significantly more shared DEGs between the combined pair bond group and short-term separation group than would be expected by chance, but this was not observed when comparing the shared genes between the combined pair bond and long-term separation group (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F Fisher's exact test: pair bond:short-term sep χ2=31.86, p=6.78 X 10–19; pair bond:long-term sep χ2=17.96, p=0.53).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test) and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F

claim: Gene expression was largely indistinguishable in short-term separated animals compared to pair bonded animals.
source: Specifically, when genes are ordered based on their degree of down- or up-regulation in the pair bond group we found that gene expression was largely indistinguishable in short-term separated animals (Rho = 0.32, p<2.2 × 10–16) and distinct from long-term separated animals (Rho = 0.048, p=1.6 × 10–7), indicating that the pair bond signature is largely eroded after prolonged separation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Spearman's correlation) and data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Gene expression in long-term separated animals is distinct from pair bonded animals, indicating that the pair bond signature is largely eroded after prolonged separation.
source: Specifically, when genes are ordered based on their degree of down- or up-regulation in the pair bond group we found that gene expression was largely indistinguishable in short-term separated animals (Rho = 0.32, p<2.2 × 10–16) and distinct from long-term separated animals (Rho = 0.048, p=1.6 × 10–7), indicating that the pair bond signature is largely eroded after prolonged separation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Spearman's correlation) and data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The pair bond:short-term Rho value indicated a stronger association than would be expected by chance.
source: We found that the pair bond:short-term Rho value indicated a stronger association than would be expected by chance (p=0.0362) while the pair bond:long term separation association value was highly likely to occur by chance (p=0.41).
evidence: Supported by permutation analysis

claim: The pair bond:long term separation association value was highly likely to occur by chance.
source: We found that the pair bond:short-term Rho value indicated a stronger association than would be expected by chance (p=0.0362) while the pair bond:long term separation association value was highly likely to occur by chance (p=0.41).
evidence: Supported by permutation analysis

claim: Extended separation erodes nucleus accumbens pair bond transcription, a potentially crucial molecular process needed to adapt to partner loss.
source: Together, these results suggest that extended separation erodes nucleus accumbens pair bond transcription, a potentially crucial molecular process needed to adapt to partner loss.
evidence: Inferred from the transcriptional data showing erosion after long-term separation

claim: The degree of overlap in the UU quadrants was greatest between the combined pair bond vs short-term separation and least between the combined pair bond vs long-term separation.
source: The degree of overlap in the UU quadrants was greatest between the combined pair bond vs short-term separation and least between the combined pair bond vs long-term separation, a result consistent with the most extensive erosion of pair bond transcription occurring after long-term separation (Figure 3F: all stats in Supplementary file 1, genes in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by RRHO analysis shown in Figure 3F

claim: Eroded UU genes are strongly upregulated in a stable pair bond and show dramatic downregulation following long-term separation.
source: The eroded UU genes are strongly upregulated in a stable pair bond and show dramatic downregulation following long-term separation (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3H

claim: The eroded UU genes and their associated biological processes may represent key aspects of adapting to partner loss.
source: Thus, the eroded UU genes and their associated biological processes may represent key aspects of adapting to partner loss.
evidence: Inferred from the expression pattern of eroded genes

claim: Transcripts in the short-term separation UU quadrant were still significantly associated, though to a lesser degree, with the pair bond associated GO terms.
source: The transcripts in the short-term separation UU quadrant were still significantly associated, though to a lesser degree, with the pair bond associated GO terms.
evidence: Based on GO analysis comparing separation timepoints to pair bond

claim: After long-term separation, the underlying transcriptional signature is much less significantly associated with the pair bond GO terms.
source: After long-term separation, the underlying transcriptional signature is much less significantly associated with the pair bond GO terms.
evidence: Based on GO analysis comparing separation timepoints to pair bond

claim: The eroded transcripts are highly associated with the pair bond associated GO terms, including glial-associated terms.
source: Further, the eroded transcripts are highly associated with the pair bond associated GO terms, including glial-associated terms.
evidence: Based on GO analysis of eroded genes

claim: Upstream regulators inducing the erosion of glial-associated genes include Sox2, estrogen receptor, Erbb3, and Ctnnb1.
source: Upstream regulators inducing the erosion of these glial-associated genes include Sox2, estrogen receptor, Erbb3, and Ctnnb1 (Figure 3J, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 3J and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: IPA pathways activated in a stable pair bond (endocannabinoid signaling, synaptogenesis, and dopamine signaling) are significantly represented among the eroded DD genes.
source: IPA pathways activated in a stable pair bond (endocannabinoid signaling, synaptogenesis, and dopamine signaling) are significantly represented among the eroded DD genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: Upstream regulators for the eroded DD transcripts include Hnf4a, Calmodulin, Hdac4, and Adora2a.
source: Upstream regulators for the eroded DD transcripts include Hnf4a, Calmodulin, Hdac4, and Adora2a (Figure 3K, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 3K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: High concordance of downregulated genes was observed between short-term and long-term partner separation.
source: In contrast to the pattern of consistently upregulated genes between the pair bond and short-term separation, we observed high concordance of downregulated genes between separation timepoints (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by RRHO analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A

claim: UU pair bond genes that are downregulated following pair bond separation are associated with dopaminergic processes.
source: We found that UU pair bond genes that are downregulated following pair bond separation are associated with dopaminergic processes and DD pair bond genes that are upregulated are associated with neuronal rearrangement processes.
evidence: Based on GO analysis of genes from separation RRHO

claim: DD pair bond genes that are upregulated following separation are associated with neuronal rearrangement processes.
source: We found that UU pair bond genes that are downregulated following pair bond separation are associated with dopaminergic processes and DD pair bond genes that are upregulated are associated with neuronal rearrangement processes.
evidence: Based on GO analysis of genes from separation RRHO

claim: The mouse and vole RPL10a cDNA sequences are 93% identical.
source: The mouse RPL10a mRNA sequence (GenBank BC083346.1) was aligned to the prairie vole RPL10a cDNA sequence (XP_005360358.1) using BLASTN 2.8.0+33. Asterisks indicate matching nucleotides. The mouse and vole cDNA sequences are 93% identical, with an expected value of 0.0.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: The mouse and vole RPL10a amino acid sequences are 100% identical.
source: The mouse RPL10a amino acid sequence was deduced from the mouse RPL10a cDNA sequence (GenBank BC083346.1) and aligned to the prairie vole RPL10a amino acid sequence (XP_005360415.1) using BLASTX 2.8.0+33. Asterisks indicate matching amino acids. The mouse and vole amino acid sequences are 100% identical, with an expected value of 3 X 10-145.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Most transcripts are depleted in the pulldown fraction as expected.
source: Differential expression analysis using the previously defined thresholds revealed that most transcripts are depleted in the pulldown fraction as expected (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: GO terms support that hSyn-vTRAP successfully isolates neuronally-enriched transcripts and filters out genes associated with gliogenesis.
source: GO terms support that hSyn-vTRAP successfully isolates neuronally-enriched transcripts and filters out genes associated with gliogenesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C

claim: Two of the most significantly positively correlated modules, blue and grey60, contain multiple neuronal genes of interest such as Drd1a, Drd2, Oprk1, Fosb, and Pdyn.
source: Of note, two of the most significantly positively correlated modules, blue and grey60, contain multiple neuronal genes of interest such as Drd1a, Drd2, Oprk1, Fosb, and Pdyn, which have previously been implicated in pair bonding and reward learning (Resendez et al., 2016; Resendez et al., 2012; Pitchers et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by WGCNA analysis and citations to Resendez et al., 2016; Resendez et al., 2012; Pitchers et al., 2010

claim: Enrichr analysis for cell type indicated that identified neuronal enriched genes are predominantly associated with the nucleus accumbens and dorsal striatum.
source: Enrichr analysis for cell type also indicated that our identified neuronal enriched genes are predominantly associated with the nucleus accumbens and dorsal striatum (Figure 4D; Chen et al., 2013; Kuleshov et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by Enrichr analysis shown in Figure 4D and citations to Chen et al., 2013; Kuleshov et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2021

claim: The neuronal enriched gene list is predominately expressed in neurons and not glia in the rat nucleus accumbens.
source: We filtered the dataset by our neuronal enriched gene list and plotted those gene's expression in the rat nucleus accumbens, which confirmed that our genes are predominately expressed in neuronal cell types (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by analysis of single nuclei NAc gene expression dataset shown in Figure 4E

claim: The strong similarity in expression validates that bulk sequencing expression can be used to infer the neuronal expression of neuronal enriched genes.
source: The strong similarity in expression validates that bulk sequencing expression can be used to infer the neuronal expression of those same genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of input and pulldown expression shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D

claim: Cluster 1 consists of genes that were upregulated in opposite-sex paired males during pair bonding and short-term separation and downregulated following long-term separation.
source: Cluster 1 consists of genes that were upregulated in opposite-sex paired males during pair bonding and short-term separation and downregulated following long-term separation.
evidence: Based on hierarchical clustering analysis of neuronal enriched genes

claim: GO terms associated with Cluster 1 include adult walking behavior, a term that contains the autism-associated gene Shank3.
source: GO terms associated with these genes include adult walking behavior, a term that contains the autism-associated gene Shank3 (Figure 4G; Gong et al., 2015; Durand et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4G and citations to Gong et al., 2015; Durand et al., 2007

claim: Cluster 2 transcripts are downregulated in pair bonded males and then robustly upregulated after short-term partner loss and, to a lesser extent, at the long-term timepoint.
source: Cluster 2 transcripts are downregulated in pair bonded males and then robustly upregulated after short-term partner loss and, to a lesser extent, at the long-term timepoint, indicating an acute transcriptional response to pair bond disruption.
evidence: Based on hierarchical clustering analysis of neuronal enriched genes

claim: GO terms associated with Cluster 2 suggest an involvement of dopaminergic systems (Drd1a and Drd2) and learning processes potentially engaged to adapt to loss.
source: The GO terms associated with these genes suggest an involvement of dopaminergic systems (Drd1a and Drd2) and learning processes potentially engaged to adapt to loss (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4G

claim: Cluster 3 contains genes that were downregulated in pair bonded males and became upregulated only after long-term opposite-sex partner separation.
source: Finally, Cluster 3 contains genes that were downregulated in pair bonded males and became upregulated only after long-term opposite-sex partner separation, representing transcripts that may help prime the vole to form a new bond.
evidence: Based on hierarchical clustering analysis of neuronal enriched genes

claim: GO terms associated with Cluster 3 are primarily implicated in cellular metabolism.
source: The GO terms associated with this cluster are primarily implicated in cellular metabolism (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4G

claim: IPA revealed that neuronal clusters 2 and 3 were enriched for estrogen receptor signaling and oxidative phosphorylation pathways.
source: IPA revealed that neuronal clusters 2 and 3 were also enriched for estrogen receptor signaling and oxidative phosphorylation pathways with cluster 2 also implicating opioid signaling pathways (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D

claim: Cluster 2 also implicates opioid signaling pathways.
source: IPA revealed that neuronal clusters 2 and 3 were also enriched for estrogen receptor signaling and oxidative phosphorylation pathways with cluster 2 also implicating opioid signaling pathways (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D

claim: Steroid and opioid signaling have been extensively implicated in pair bonding.
source: Steroid and opioid signaling have been extensively implicated in pair bonding (Resendez et al., 2016; Resendez et al., 2012; Loth and Donaldson, 2021; Inoue et al., 2013; Stetzik et al., 2018; Carter and Perkeybile, 2018; Lei et al., 2010; Cushing et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Resendez et al., 2016; Resendez et al., 2012; Loth and Donaldson, 2021; Inoue et al., 2013; Stetzik et al., 2018; Carter and Perkeybile, 2018; Lei et al., 2010; Cushing et al., 2008

claim: Pair bonding leads to consistent and persistent shifts in NAc transcription, which erode as a function of long-term partner separation.
source: We show that, in the absence of new bonding opportunities, the original pair bond will persist for at least 4 weeks post-partner-separation. However, prior work indicates that there is still an adaptive process occurring within this time frame that primes a vole to form a new bond if available (Harbert et al., 2020). Our work suggests that this adaptation is mediated at least in part by an erosion of bond-related transcription in mesolimbic systems that largely precedes bond dissolution at the behavioral level.
evidence: Inferred from the combined behavioral and transcriptional data, with citation to Harbert et al., 2020

claim: The original pair bond will persist for at least 4 weeks post-partner-separation in the absence of new bonding opportunities.
source: We show that, in the absence of new bonding opportunities, the original pair bond will persist for at least 4 weeks post-partner-separation.
evidence: Based on behavioral data from the study

claim: Erosion of bond-related transcription in mesolimbic systems largely precedes bond dissolution at the behavioral level.
source: Our work suggests that this adaptation is mediated at least in part by an erosion of bond-related transcription in mesolimbic systems that largely precedes bond dissolution at the behavioral level.
evidence: Inferred from the combined behavioral and transcriptional data

claim: The partner preference test may be insufficient to capture the uniquely rewarding aspect of pair bonds compared with other affiliative relationships.
source: The partner preference test, as employed in our study, may be insufficient to capture the uniquely rewarding aspect of pair bonds compared with other affiliative relationships such as sibling relationships (Goodwin et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculation based on study results and citation to Goodwin et al., 2019

claim: Pair bonds strengthen and mature over extended cohabitation periods, which may contribute to the observed perseverance of partner preference for weeks after separation.
source: As demonstrated here and in other studies, pair bonds strengthen and mature over extended cohabitation periods, which may contribute to the observed perseverance of partner preference for weeks after separation (Scribner et al., 2020; Brusman et al., 2021).
evidence: Inferred from study results and supported by citations to Scribner et al., 2020; Brusman et al., 2021

claim: Partner preference in males is not affected by female ovariectomy.
source: However, partner preference in males is not affected by female ovariectomy (Curtis, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Curtis, 2010

claim: Male voles remember and express selective affiliation despite prolonged isolation.
source: Regardless, our results suggest that male voles remember and express selective affiliation despite prolonged isolation, though partner separation impedes the ongoing bond strengthening.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral data

claim: Stable transcriptional changes are critical to maintain different behavioral states.
source: Prior work on social dominance suggests that such stable transcriptional changes are critical to maintain different behavioral states (Cardoso et al., 2015; Zayed and Robinson, 2012; Tripp et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cardoso et al., 2015; Zayed and Robinson, 2012; Tripp et al., 2018

claim: This is the first demonstration that stable transcriptional changes may maintain mature pair bonds.
source: However, to our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a similar conceptual underpinning may maintain mature pair bonds.
evidence: Based on the novelty of the study findings

claim: Pair bonding and separation induce neuronal plasticity and synapse re-organization, which require large amounts of energy and induce mitochondrial redistribution within neurons.
source: Together, these terms implicate processes central to neuronal remodeling and synaptic plasticity. Of note, while our analyses do identify a number of mitochondrial GO terms, these terms are not as strongly implicated in our analyses as in previous reports (Duclot et al., 2020). Despite this, our study confirms a potential role for mitochondrial dynamics in the NAc in male prairie vole pair bonding. This is consistent with a model in which pair bonding and separation induce neuronal plasticity and synapse re-organization, which require large amounts of energy and induce mitochondrial redistribution within neurons (Ülgen et al., 2023).
evidence: Inferred from GO analysis results and supported by citations to Duclot et al., 2020 and Ülgen et al., 2023

claim: Transcripts associated with gliogenesis, glial cell differentiation, and myelination are upregulated in stable pair bonds.
source: Transcripts associated with gliogenesis, glial cell differentiation, and myelination are upregulated in stable pair bonds, potentially reflecting the importance of glial cells in sculpting and refining neural circuits in response to social experience (Loth and Donaldson, 2021; Kopec et al., 2018; Pohl et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on GO analysis and supported by citations to Loth and Donaldson, 2021; Kopec et al., 2018; Pohl et al., 2021

claim: Hypomyelination and oligodendrocyte dysfunction are seen in mice and rats after chronic social defeat or chronic social isolation and in individuals with depression.
source: Hypomyelination and oligodendrocyte dysfunction are seen in mice and rats after chronic social defeat or chronic social isolation and in individuals with depression (Bonnefil et al., 2019; Lehmann et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonnefil et al., 2019; Lehmann et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2021

claim: Social reintroduction rescued hypomyelination in mice.
source: This appears reversible as social reintroduction rescued hypomyelination in mice (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012

claim: One mechanism for social deprivation-mediated hypomyelination and impaired oligodendrocyte maturation is by reduced flux through Erbb3-based signaling pathways.
source: One mechanism for social deprivation-mediated hypomyelination and impaired oligodendrocyte maturation is by reduced flux through Erbb3-based signaling pathways (Liu et al., 2012; Makinodan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2012; Makinodan et al., 2012

claim: Erbb3 is one of 24 genes whose differential expression is conserved in taxonomically diverse monogamous species when compared to closely related non-monogamous relatives.
source: Of note, Erbb3 is one of 24 genes whose differential expression is conserved in taxonomically diverse monogamous species when compared to closely related non-monogamous relatives (Young et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Young et al., 2019

claim: Erbb3 is upregulated during pair bonding through short-term separation but is no longer upregulated following long-term separation.
source: We find Erbb3 upregulated during pair bonding through short-term separation but it is no longer upregulated following long-term separation.
evidence: Based on transcriptional data from the study

claim: IPA analysis indicates that Erbb3 is an upstream regulator of the eroded genes.
source: Further, IPA analysis indicates that Erbb3 is an upstream regulator of the eroded genes.
evidence: Based on IPA analysis

claim: Long-term separation may be downregulating Erbb3-associated pathways resulting in reduced myelination and disrupting oligodendrocytes specifically in opposite-sex-separated animals.
source: Thus, it is possible that long-term separation is downregulating Erbb3-associated pathways resulting in reduced myelination and disrupting oligodendrocytes specifically in opposite-sex-separated animals.
evidence: Speculation based on the combined evidence from transcriptional data and literature

claim: Dopamine associated genes in cluster #2 are robustly upregulated in neurons after short-term partner loss, possibly reflecting a withdrawal-like state.
source: Notably, dopamine associated genes in cluster #2 are robustly upregulated in neurons after short-term partner loss, possibly reflecting a withdrawal-like state (Potretzke and Ryabinin, 2019; Young et al., 2008; Lieberwirth and Wang, 2016).
evidence: Based on neuronal enriched gene analysis and supported by citations to Potretzke and Ryabinin, 2019; Young et al., 2008; Lieberwirth and Wang, 2016

claim: Genes associated with anxiety and energy production in cluster #3 are upregulated only after long-term partner loss, possibly to facilitate seeking a new partner.
source: Genes associated with anxiety and energy production in cluster #3 are upregulated only after long-term partner loss, possibly to facilitate seeking a new partner.
evidence: Based on neuronal enriched gene analysis

claim: The substantial erosion of pair bond transcription in the NAc after long-term separation is not matched by a similar reduction in partner-directed affiliative behaviors.
source: A notable aspect of our results is that the substantial erosion of pair bond transcription in the NAc after long-term separation is not matched by a similar reduction in partner-directed affiliative behaviors, despite evidence that changes in gene expression in this brain region help maintain bonds over time (Aragona and Wang, 2004; Aragona et al., 2006; Aragona et al., 2003).
evidence: Based on the combined behavioral and transcriptional data, with citations to Aragona and Wang, 2004; Aragona et al., 2006; Aragona et al., 2003

claim: Other brain regions such as the ventral tegmental area, medial pre-frontal cortex, and the hippocampus innervate the NAc and have known roles in social behavior.
source: Specifically, the ventral tegmental area, medial pre-frontal cortex, and the hippocampus innervate the NAc and have known roles in social behavior. Transcriptional dynamics may differ within these regions, potentially contributing to bond persistence (Okuyama et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2016; Kogan et al., 2000; Amadei et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okuyama et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2016; Kogan et al., 2000; Amadei et al., 2017

claim: Pair bond transcription may induce other long-term biological changes that erode more slowly, including long-lasting epigenetic memory as well as proteomic and/or structural changes.
source: In addition, pair bond transcription may induce other long-term biological changes that erode more slowly. These include long-lasting epigenetic memory as well as proteomic and/or structural changes that may contribute to behavioral persistence (Tuesta and Zhang, 2014; Nestler et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to Tuesta and Zhang, 2014; Nestler et al., 2016

claim: Oxytocin signaling in the NAc is required for pair bond formation and maintenance in male prairie voles.
source: Finally, oxytocin signaling in the NAc is required for pair bond formation and maintenance in male prairie voles (Johnson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2016

claim: Recent publication of pair bond formation in Oxtr null voles provides a unique opportunity to identify oxytocin-dependent and independent transcriptional changes that support pair bonds.
source: Recent publication of pair bond formation in Oxtr null voles provides a unique opportunity to identify oxytocin-dependent and independent transcriptional changes that support pair bonds (Berendzen and Manoli, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berendzen and Manoli, 2022

claim: Wild male voles who lose a partner will remain at the nest for approximately 17 days.
source: Consistent with our laboratory observations, wild male voles who lose a partner will remain at the nest for ~17 days (Tamarin et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tamarin et al., 1990

claim: All females in opposite-sex pairs were tubally ligated to avoid confounds of pregnancy, but to keep the ovaries intact as to not impact hormonal function.
source: All females in opposite-sex pairs were tubally ligated to avoid confounds of pregnancy, but to keep the ovaries intact as to not impact hormonal function.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Sexually naive adult prairie voles (N=219: 161 M, 58 F, P60 - P168 at experiment start) were used in the study.
source: Sexually naive adult prairie voles (Microtus ochrogaster, N=219: 161 M, 58 F, P60 - P168 at experiment start) were bred in-house in a colony originating from a cross between voles obtained from colonies at Emory University and University of California Davis, both of which were established from wild animals collected in Illinois.
evidence: Description of experimental subjects

source: All procedures were performed in accordance with standard ethical guidelines (National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals) and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the University of Colorado Boulder (protocol #2435).
